stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: Low hemoglobin with macrocytosis and a low vitamin B12 level.
options.B: Low hemoglobin with normocytosis and an elevated ferritin level in an inflammatory state.
options.C: Normal hemoglobin with macrocytosis and increased body iron stores.
options.D: Low hemoglobin with microcytosis and a low ferritin level.

rationale: ARUP Consult states that iron deficiency anemia is caused by low body iron stores. As deficiency progresses, anemia commonly becomes microcytic, and a low serum ferritin supports depleted iron stores in the appropriate clinical context. Ferritin can be elevated by inflammation, so it should not be interpreted in isolation when inflammatory disease is present. Therefore D is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia. A is more consistent with vitamin B12 deficiency, B better fits anemia of inflammation, and C does not describe iron-deficiency anemia.
educational_objective: Recognize low hemoglobin with microcytosis and low ferritin as a characteristic laboratory pattern of iron deficiency anemia while interpreting ferritin in clinical context because inflammation can increase it.
source_document_title: Iron Deficiency Anemia; Anemia of Chronic Disease/Anemia of Inflammation
source_version_date: Iron Deficiency Anemia and ACD/AI topics updated October 2025; live currentness rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Iron Deficiency Anemia: initial testing includes Hb/Hct, RBC indices including MCV, then ferritin; iron deficiency is low body iron stores. ACD/AI differential table: IDA typically low MCV and low ferritin; ACD/AI typically normal MCV and high ferritin. Ferritin interpretation is complicated by inflammation.
source_claim_supported: Iron deficiency anemia commonly presents with low hemoglobin, low MCV as deficiency progresses, and low ferritin reflecting depleted iron stores; inflammation can complicate ferritin interpretation.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret CBC/red-cell indices and iron studies, recognize abnormal patterns, and distinguish hematologic causes requiring further evaluation.

source_original.stem: Which laboratory pattern is most consistent with iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: Low hemoglobin with macrocytosis and a low vitamin B12 level.

options.C: Normal hemoglobin with macrocytosis and increased body iron stores.

source_original.rationale: Iron deficiency anemia commonly produces low hemoglobin and microcytosis, and a low ferritin level supports depleted iron stores. Ferritin must still be interpreted in clinical context because inflammation and other conditions can raise it.
source_original.source_detail: Laboratory evaluation: low hemoglobin, microcytosis as deficiency progresses, and low ferritin supporting depleted iron stores. correction_summary: Retained the iron-deficiency laboratory-pattern construct and key D. Added the inflammation caveat from current ARUP guidance and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a standard CBC/ferritin pattern with clinically relevant interpretation context.

audit_findings.exact_locator: ARUP IDA initial evaluation and ACD/AI versus IDA differential table
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the characteristic low-Hb/low-MCV/low-ferritin pattern and explicitly avoids treating ferritin as context-free in inflammatory states.

distractor_audit.A: More consistent with vitamin B12-associated macrocytic anemia.
distractor_audit.B: Normocytosis with elevated ferritin in inflammation is more consistent with ACD/AI than uncomplicated IDA.
distractor_audit.C: Does not represent anemia or depleted iron stores.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D combines anemia, microcytosis, and depleted iron stores without an alternative explanatory pattern.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are coherent hematologic laboratory patterns.
